newsitem.title: FRANCE: Relatives of TWA crash dead begin painful voyage.
newsitem.headline: Relatives of TWA crash dead begin painful voyage.

text.p: Some 120 relatives of French victims of last year's TWA Flight 800 crash began a painful voyage to New York on Wednesday for ceremonies marking the air disaster's first anniversary.
About 80 of the family members accepted an offer by TWA to fly them to New York while another 40 travelled on a separate Air France flight.

"It's an extremely painful moment. At the same time it's a way to pay tribute to the 230 victims of Flight 800," said Michelle Richter of Clermont-Ferrand in central France as she prepared to board her flight to New York at Paris' Charles de Gaulle airport.
"Every moment of our lives we have memories. We will have to live with the suffering until the end of our days," Richter told Reuters. She lost two teenage daughters in the crash.

The Paris-bound Boeing jumbo jet exploded on July 17, 1996 off the coast of Long Island minutes after taking off from New York's Kennedy International Airport. All 230 passengers and crew on board were killed, including 45 French nationals.

Suspicion initially centred on a possible terrorist attack. But investigators now believe the explosion was caused by a technical problem and not a missile or bomb, though no official conclusion has been reached by crash probers.
To commemorate the anniversary, a mass will be held at St. Patrick's Cathedral in New York City followed by a ceremony on a Long Island beach near the crash site.
Relatives of the victims will also meet crash investigators and be given the opportunity to ask questions about the official inquiry.

Marc Cayrol of Montpellier in southern France, who lost a brother in the crash, said the voyage would be painful but it was important to honour the dead and "to let investigators know we will press them until we get the truth."

"It's a painful trip because we are going back to where we were one year ago. Personally I waited there 18 days before they found the remains of my brother. So it was painful then and today it will be painful to go back to that place," he said.

Cayrol said he was convinced the crash was due to a technical problem but acknowledged that some relatives still believed it might have been caused by a missile or a bomb, conclusions which have been ruled out by investigators.
Crash probers now know that an explosion ripped through the jet's nearly empty, but vapour-filled, centre fuel tank, but they do not know what caused the explosion.
Because the official cause has not been determined, Cayrol said he feared that U.S. aviation safety agencies would not order safety measures to avoid a repetition of the Flight 800 disaster.
"It's a problem of fuel vapours in the centre fuel tank which exploded," he said.
